connections.feedback: Yes. Rain makes the streets wet and also makes people carry umbrellas. When one hidden cause produces two things, the two things move together without one causing the other.
A few drips from umbrellas cannot wet a whole street. Look at what else happens on those days instead.
The streets are wet because of the weather, not because people decided on umbrellas first. The order of events does not fit.
More days of data are never a bad idea, but here a likely third cause is already sitting in plain sight. Waiting skips the easiest explanation.
connections.notes: Cautious about the data, but passes over an obvious third factor.

Comparing starting grades would test the idea directly, which is a strength. It takes effort, and it answers the question only if the records exist.

connections.feedback: Yes. A fair coin has no memory. Each flip is a fresh start, so the next flip is still about even, even after five heads.
This is the idea that results must balance out soon. The coin does not remember earlier flips, so tails is not owed.
Five in a row happens by chance fairly often. It is a reason to look, not proof that the coin is unfair.
Checking the coin and flipping more times is a sensible way to settle it. Five heads alone is weak evidence, so it is more a curiosity than a concern.
connections.notes: Reasonable to check; five flips is thin evidence.
